title: Causes and Conduct of World War II
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: At the Munich Conference of September 1938, Britain and France agreed to let Hitler annex a large part of Czechoslovakia in exchange for his promise of no further demands. Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain claimed he had secured 'peace for our time'; less than a year later Hitler invaded Poland.

Appeasement — conceding to Hitler's demands to avoid war — failed catastrophically because it convinced him the democracies were weak and would not fight. Rather than satisfying the aggressor, it emboldened further aggression.

World War II was the deadliest conflict in human history, killing an estimated 60 to 80 million people, more than three times the toll of World War I. Unlike WWI, the majority of the dead were civilians, not soldiers.

The long-term causes of WWII were the unresolved tensions of WWI: the bitter, vengeful legacy of the Treaty of Versailles, the global devastation of the Great Depression, and the rise of aggressive, expansionist totalitarian regimes that saw conquest as the path to national greatness.

The immediate causes of WWII included a chain of Axis aggressions in the 1930s: Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931 and China in 1937, Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935, and Nazi Germany rearmed, remilitarized the Rhineland, annexed Austria, and seized Czechoslovakia.

The Nazi-Soviet Pact (1939) was a cynical non-aggression agreement between Hitler and Stalin to divide Eastern Europe between them. It cleared the way for Germany's invasion of Poland and was later broken when Germany invaded the USSR in 1941.

World War II in Europe began on September 1, 1939, when Germany invaded Poland, prompting Britain and France to declare war. The invasion was the immediate trigger of a war made likely by long-term tensions and failed appeasement.

Germany used blitzkrieg ('lightning war') — fast, coordinated assaults by tanks, aircraft, and infantry — to conquer Poland and then France and much of Western Europe by 1940, a sharp contrast with the trench stalemate of WWI.

In 1941 Hitler invaded the Soviet Union, opening a colossal and savage Eastern Front where the bulk of the war's fighting and dying took place. The Soviet victory at the Battle of Stalingrad (1942–43) became the turning point of the war in Europe; the USSR suffered roughly 27 million dead.

The Western Allies opened a second front with the D-Day landings in Normandy in June 1944, squeezing Germany between advancing American-British forces in the west and Soviet armies in the east until Germany surrendered in May 1945.

Japan's surprise attack on the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor in December 1941 brought the United States fully into World War II. The U.S. then fought back across the Pacific in a brutal island-hopping campaign.

Japan sought to build a vast empire (the 'Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere'), conquering much of Southeast Asia and the Pacific. The Battle of Midway (1942) was the turning point of the Pacific war, halting Japanese expansion.

The two alliances in WWII were the Axis (Germany, Italy, and Japan) and the Allies, led by Britain, the Soviet Union, the United States, and China. As in WWI, both sides drew on global empires and colonial troops.

World War II carried total war to an extreme: the deliberate mass targeting of civilians became central. Most of the roughly 60–80 million dead were civilians, killed through bombing, occupation, starvation, and genocide.

Strategic bombing deliberately attacked enemy cities to destroy industry and break civilian morale. Examples include the German Blitz against British cities and the far more destructive Allied firebombing of Hamburg, Dresden, and Tokyo, which killed tens of thousands in single nights.

Occupation regimes, especially Nazi Germany's in Eastern Europe and Japan's in China and Southeast Asia, were murderously brutal — marked by massacres, forced labor, starvation, and systematic atrocities such as the Rape of Nanjing.

The Holocaust was the Nazi regime's deliberate, industrialized genocide of six million Jews, along with millions of Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners, and political prisoners — a state-organized program of mass murder using ghettos, mass shootings, and death camps.

To force Japan's surrender and avoid a costly invasion, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, killing well over a hundred thousand people, mostly civilians. Japan surrendered days later, and the nuclear shadow hung over the entire Cold War.

World War II ended with the old European great powers exhausted or destroyed and two superpowers standing astride a ruined world: the United States, with its homeland untouched and economy supercharged, and the Soviet Union, which controlled Eastern Europe. Their rivalry became the Cold War.

World War II accelerated the end of European empires: the colonial powers were weakened and discredited, millions of colonial subjects had fought in a war against tyranny, and Japan's early conquests shattered the myth of European invincibility in Asia, fueling decolonization.

WWII produced new institutions designed to prevent its recurrence: the United Nations, replacing the failed League of Nations; new global economic institutions; and, in response to the Holocaust, a new international language of human rights and the concept of 'genocide.'

Comparing the world wars: both were global total wars mobilizing whole societies and colonial empires, driven by nationalism and industrial technology. But WWII was far deadlier, killed mostly civilians, featured deliberate genocide and strategic bombing, used mobile blitzkrieg rather than trench stalemate, and ended with atomic weapons and two superpowers.
